Subject: Dental Materials
Question: The process in which a material melts to form a crystalline phase and a liquid phase known as
Explanation: Incongruent melting is the process by which one material melts to form a liquid plus a different crystalline material. An example is feldspar. One of the important properties of feldspar is its tendency to form crystalline leucite (K2O.Al2O3.4SiO2) when melted. Leucite is a potassium-aluminum-silicate mineral with a high coefficient of thermal expansion (20 to 25 x 10^-6/K) compared with feldspar glasses that have much lower coefficients of thermal expansion (8.6 x 10^-6/K). When feldspar is heated at temperatures between 1150°C and 1530°C, it undergoes incongruent melting to form crystals of leucite in a liquid glass. This tendency of feldspar to form leucite during incongruent melting controls thermal expansion during the use of porcelains for metal bonding. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.430]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Tear strength of which is least?
Explanation: Poly sulphides have highest tear strength followed by polyether, condensation silicone and addition silicone. The ranking of tear strength from the lowest to highest of the impression materials: Silicones (addition and condensation) < Polyether < Polysulfide. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.170,172 / Dental Materials by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.178,183,239,245]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Hardener in gypsum is
Explanation: Both agar and alginate impression materials retard the setting reaction of gypsum products. In addition, a small percentage of borax is added to strengthen the agar gel; borax also acts as a potent retarder for the setting of gypsum. After an agar impression is taken, excess is trimmed and the impression is stored in 2% potassium sulfate (accelerator/hardener), which controls water volume and gives better surface integrity to the stone for 5 to 20 minutes. The potassium sulfate solution gives a harder surface to the stone die material. Alginate materials are added with 3% potassium titanium fluoride by the manufacturer as a gypsum hardener/accelerator. Die materials have less resistance to abrasion; attempts have been made to increase the hardness of gypsum products by incorporation of the set gypsum with methylmethacrylate that is allowed to polymerize, which increases strength and hardness. A wetting agent such as "lignosulfates" is added to reduce the water requirement of a stone and enable production of harder, stronger, denser set gypsum. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.164]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Stearic acid is added in impression compound for
Explanation: Impression compounds are composed of a mixture of waxes, thermoplastic resins, filler, and a coloring agent. The waxes or resins are the principal ingredients of the matrix. Filler is added to increase the viscosity at temperatures above that of the mouth and to increase the rigidity of the compound at room temperature. Shellac, stearic acid, and gutta-percha are added to improve plasticity and workability. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.178]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Fins in casting are seen
Explanation: Too rapid heating will cause cracking of the investment. In such a case, the outside layer of the investment expands much more than the center sections; consequently the outside layer starts to expand thermally, resulting in compressive stress in the outside layer, which counteracts tensile stresses in the middle regions of the mold. Such a stress distribution causes the brittle investment to crack from the interior to outward in the form of radial cracks. The molten alloy flows into these cracks and produces a casting with fins or spines. This condition is especially likely with a cristobalite investment. The comparatively low inversion temperature of cristobalite and the rapid rate of expansion during the inversion make it especially important to heat the investment slowly. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.218]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Size of ZnPo4 used for luting?
Explanation: The film thickness of an ideal luting cement should be less than or equal to 25 µm. According to ADA specification number 8 for type I (luting) Zinc phosphate cement, the film thickness is less than or equal to 25 µm. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.307,311 / Dental Materials Science by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.102]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Strength of gypsum products is generally expressed in terms of?
Explanation: The strength of set gypsum products is generally expressed in terms of compressive strength, although diametral tensile strength should also be considered to determine the overall strength characteristics. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.188]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Stiffness is related to?
Explanation: Stiffness or rigidity may be defined as the resistance of a material to elastic deformation. Generally, the materials with highest elastic modulus are considered as stiffest. The term elastic modulus represents the relative stiffness or rigidity of a material within the elastic range. [Dental Materials Science by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.19]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Varnish is used under which cement?
Explanation: A cavity varnish must be used to protect the pulp from the acidic components that are released from overlying cement bases like zinc phosphate cements. When a cavity varnish or dentin bonding agent is indicated to seal a restoration, the base often governs the order of material application. If a zinc phosphate cement base is used, a sealing (varnish) material should be applied to the cavity walls before placement of the base. For the more biocompatible cement base materials (e.g., calcium hydroxide, ZOE, polycarboxylate, and GIC), the base cement is placed, followed by the cavity varnish after the base has hardened. For resin-based composites, calcium hydroxide and GIC are satisfactory base cements. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.316]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Most common problem faced with single etch adhesive system is
Explanation: In recent years, the etching step of dental structures has been merged with the priming and bonding steps, giving rise to the self-etch strategy one-bottle self-etch adhesives. The etchant, the primer and the adhesive resin have been incorporated into one bottle, resulting in single-step application, which allows simultaneous etching and priming of tooth structures with one adhesive component. Previous studies have attributed unfavorable bond defects, including nanoleakage, water trees, bubbles, and phase separation at adhesive resin-tooth interfaces of all-in-one and one-bottle adhesives to their high water content. Phase separation may take place due to hydrolytic instability of self-etch adhesive systems. [Fundamentals of Operative Dentistry by Summit 3rd ed, p.226]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Incomplete casting is due to
Explanation: Incomplete casting is due to incomplete filling of mold by molten alloy. The common causes which inhibit the ingress of the liquefied metal are: insufficient venting (if the air cannot be vented quickly, the molten alloy does not fill the mold before it solidifies); high viscosity of metal due to insufficient heating; incomplete elimination of wax residues from the mold — if too many products of combustion remain in the mold, the pores in the investment may become filled so that the air cannot be vented completely; and narrow sprue diameter, etc. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.227-228]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: ZOE is made eugenol free by
Explanation: One of the chief disadvantages of ZOE pastes is the possible stinging or burning sensation caused by the eugenol as it leaches out and contacts soft tissues. Zinc oxide can react with various carboxylic acids and form ZOE-like materials. Orthoethoxybenzoic acid (EBA) is a valuable substitute for eugenol in this regard. Bactericidal agents and other medicaments can also be incorporated without interfering with the reaction. Orthophosphoric acid is used as liquid in zinc phosphate cements; poly acrylic acid is used as liquid in zinc polycarboxylate and glass ionomer cements. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.197]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Coupling agent present in composite
Explanation: Composition of dental composites includes coupling agents, which act as bonding agents between fillers and the resin matrix, e.g., gamma-methacryloxy propyl trimethoxysilane, an organosilane. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.278]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Shape of stainless steel wire determine
Explanation: Stiffness is the measure of the force required to bend or otherwise deform the material to a definite distance; it is the rate of force delivery required for inactivation. Stiffness is proportional to the modulus of elasticity and cross-section (shape/geometry) of a given wire and is not appreciably influenced by any hardening treatment. Stiffness and springiness are reciprocal properties: Stiffness = 1/Springiness. Factors affecting stiffness, strength and range include the mechanical arrangement (e.g., length of archwire), the form of the wire itself (size and shape of cross-section, i.e., geometry), and the material/alloy composition and hardness. [Khamatkar A, Ideal Properties of Orthodontic Wires and their Clinical Implications – A Review, IOSR Journal of Dental and Medical Sciences, 2015;14(1):47-50]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Temperature for brazing is
Explanation: Soldering, brazing, and welding are all methods of joining two or more pieces of metal. In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastics) must be similar; welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. Brazing is a group of joining processes that produce coalescence of materials by heating them to the brazing temperature and using a filler metal (solder) having a liquidus above 840°F (450°C), and below the solidus of the base metals. Soldering is a low-temperature analog to brazing; soldering takes place with fillers that melt at below 840°F (450°C). In dentistry, many metals are joined by brazing, although the term soldering is commonly used. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.367]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Most common accelerator in gypsum is
Explanation: The chemical that increases the rate of hemihydrate dissolution or precipitation of dihydrate accelerates the setting reaction. The most commonly used accelerator is potassium sulfate, which is particularly effective in concentrations greater than 2%. Other accelerators: slurry water, NaCl (2%), Sodium Sulfate (3.4%). Retarders: ABCs (Acetates, Borates and Citrates). Borax acts as a retarder for setting of gypsum products; however, borax at a concentration less than 0.2 mM (about 0.08 g/L) acts as an accelerator. Greater than 2% NaCl and more than 12% of Sodium sulphate act as retarders. Colloidal systems like blood, saliva, and hydrocolloid impression materials also act as retarders. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.186 / Dental Materials Science by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.239]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Most common accelerator added to gypsum product
Explanation: Repeat from previous session — see explanation for Q17: potassium sulfate is the most commonly used accelerator for gypsum products, particularly effective at concentrations greater than 2%.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Crocus cloth is
Explanation: Crocus cloth is an abrasive sheet similar to sand paper covered with a layer of very fine loose ferric oxide glued to one side. It is used for fine abrading or polishing. Emery is a mixture of aluminium oxide (Corundum) and iron. Garnet is a silicate mineral with a combination of other minerals such as Al, Co, Mg, Fe and Mn. Pumice contains silica as a major ingredient. Rouge is a fine red powder composed of iron oxide. [Anusavice 9th ed, p.562]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Wax used in inlay cast metal fabrication
Explanation: Inlay wax is a type of pattern wax available in sticks, cakes, blocks, in various colors (blue, green, purple). Uses: preparation of wax pattern for cast metal restorations like inlays, onlays, crowns, bridges. Types: Type I (soft) for indirect technique; Type II (hard) for direct technique. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.195]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: A copolymer which has a direct chain of one type and branches of other type is called a
Explanation:
The polymer which is composed of more than one type of repeat unit is called a copolymer, and its process of formation is known as copolymerization.

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Alternating Copolymers | Different types of monomers in a polymer are distributed alternatively throughout the chain. |
| Random Copolymers | Different monomer units in a polymer are distributed in random throughout the chain; the polymer is called random copolymer. |
| Block Copolymer | When a block of one repeat unit is followed by a block of another repeat unit, which in turn is followed by the first repeat unit, and the polymer is called block polymer. |
| Graft Copolymer | Graft copolymers are branched molecules where the main chain is made entirely of one repeat unit, while the branched chains are made of yet another repeating end. |

[Dental Materials by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.55]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: From clinical point of view, property of composite is to provide
Explanation: Translucency is a property of substances that permits the passage of light but disperses the light, so objects cannot be seen through the material. Tooth enamel has inherent translucency, thus the task in dentistry is finding an esthetic dental restoration that has translucency properties similar to human enamel. To render a restoration imperceptible, appropriate levels of translucency are required; this characteristic can be idealized by harmonizing the optical properties of the restoration with those of the adjacent natural teeth. Composite resins tend to produce natural-looking restorations largely because they are relatively translucent. The translucency of dental resin composites depends on their thickness and the scattering and absorption coefficients of the resin, filler particles, pigments, and opacifiers. Thus, the inherent translucency of the material may contribute to matching the shade of the underlying tooth and the tooth adjacent to it. They provide a "chameleon" effect in small restorations, allowing the adjacent and underlying tooth structure to reflect or show through the restoration. [Comparative Translucency of Esthetic Composite Resin Restorative Materials. J Can Dent Assoc 2010;76:a84]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In Co-Cr alloy, function of chromium is to provide
Explanation: Base metal alloys generally comprise the group of cast metals that rely on chromium for corrosion resistance. Chromium on the surface of the alloy rapidly oxidizes to form a thin layer of chromium oxide, which prevents the diffusion of oxygen into the underlying metals and improves its corrosion resistance. Chromium also strengthens the alloy by solution hardening. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.375]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Green shrinkage occurs in
Explanation: During the drying process of ethyl silicate investment material, the gel loses alcohol and water to form a concentrated, hard gel. As might be expected, a volumetric contraction accompanies the drying, which reduces the size of the mold. This contraction is known as 'green shrinkage', which is additive to the setting shrinkage. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.210]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Microwave curing of acrylic resin depicts
Explanation: Polymerization of acrylic resins can be accomplished by chemical activation, visible light activation or heating activation using hot water or microwave energy. Microwave oven is a device in which electromagnetic waves are produced by a generator called a magnetron, which is used to generate heat. Microwave heating is independent of thermal conductivity. Microwave radiation as a high-frequency electromagnetic wave exerts its function by frictional heating from its interaction with polar molecules; water molecules are polar molecules with the hydrogen side carrying a positive charge and the oxygen side carrying a negative charge. When microwave radiation hits the water molecules, they oscillate between two and five billion times to align themselves with the fluctuating microwave, and this rapid molecular rotation generates and uniformly distributes heat. Methylmethacrylate monomer molecules are also polar molecules and microwave energy heats them similarly. Advantages of microwave curing: saves time from several hours to few minutes; cleaner curing as it does not need water; better bond strength with acrylic teeth; equal or better dimensional accuracy; more color stability under conditions of accelerated aging; can also be used successfully with metallic removable partial denture frameworks. [Comparative evaluation of surface porosities in conventional heat polymerized acrylic resin cured by water bath and microwave energy with microwavable acrylic resin cured by microwave energy. Contemp Clin Dent 2013 Apr-Jun;4(2):147-151]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Indium in metal are further added to
Explanation: Minute amounts of oxidizable elements such as iron, tin, and indium are added to high noble (HN) and noble (N) alloys used for metal-ceramic prostheses to promote bonding between the ceramic veneer and the metal oxide on the metal surface. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.72]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: The property common in amalgam and ceramic
Option A: Low compressive strength and high tensile strength
Option B: High compressive strength and low tensile strength
Option D: High compressive and high tensile strength
Explanation: Both amalgam and ceramics are brittle in nature. All brittle materials are good under compression and poor under tensile loads. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.377]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Wettability is increased by
Option C: It is directly proportional to contact angle
Option D: Adhesive forces are more important than cohesive
Explanation: Wettability refers to how well a liquid spreads on a solid surface. It is influenced by surface energy (also called surface tension) and the contact angle (θ) between the liquid and the solid. Higher surface energy of a solid makes it more "attractive" to liquids, improving wettability. Wettability is inversely related to contact angle (lower θ = better wettability). Complete wetting occurs at a contact angle of 0° and no wetting occurs at an angle of 180°. Option D — adhesive forces are more important than cohesive — is partially true, but not the best answer; wettability improves when adhesive forces (liquid-solid) dominate over cohesive forces (liquid-liquid), but this is a consequence of high surface energy. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.26]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Type II ZOE is
Option C: Long term luting agent for fixed prosthesis
Option D: Can be used as a base
Explanation: According to ADA specification number 30, ZOE cements are classified as: Type I — Temporary luting cement for fixed prosthesis; Type II — Long-term luting cement for fixed prosthesis; Type III — Temporary restoration and thermal insulating base; Type IV — Intermediate restoration, cavity liner and chemical insulator. [Dental Materials by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.93]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Strength of gypsum can be measured with
Explanation: Universal testing machine is most commonly used apparatus to measure compressive, tensile, shear and flexural strength of most of the dental materials. Gillmore needles and vicat penetrometers are used for measuring the setting time of gypsum products. Kreb's penetrometer is used for measuring the setting time of ZOE impression pastes.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Putty wash technique is utilized for
Explanation: The chemical ingredient used in condensation silicone is Hydroxyl terminated polydimethylsiloxane. Putty-wash technique was originally developed for condensation silicone to minimize the effect of associated dimensional changes. The thick putty material is placed in a stock tray and a preliminary impression is made. This preliminary impression is used as a custom tray, either by cutting away some of the "tray" putty or by using a thin polyethylene sheet as a spacer between the putty and the prepared teeth during the preliminary impression making. A mixture of the thin-consistency wash material is placed into the putty impression and on the preparation; then the tray is reseated in the mouth to make the final impression. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.159,160]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is radiopaque
Explanation: Radiopacity of impression materials mainly depends on the composition and thickness of an impression material. Among four elastomeric impression materials, polysulfide materials show more radiopacity due to the presence of Lead dioxide. Among the different viscosities of elastomeric impression materials, putty body materials depict more radiopacity followed by heavy, medium and light body materials. [Mota GE et al. Radiopacity of impression materials using an indirect digital system, Rev Odontocienc., 2008;23(4):333-337]

Question: Crocus cloth is
Explanation: Repeat from previous session — see explanation for Q19: Crocus cloth is covered with a layer of very fine loose ferric oxide, i.e., rouge.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Corrosion product of high copper amalgam
Explanation: Low-copper amalgams: Low-copper amalgams form corrosion products of tin oxides and tin chlorides at both the tooth/amalgam interface (to seal the margins and prevent leakage) and in the interior of the amalgam. The most corrosion-prone phase in these alloys is gamma 2 (Sn8Hg). High-copper amalgams: High-copper amalgams form corrosion products similar to those formed by the low-copper alloys (tin oxides and tin chlorides); in addition they form copper chloride. They corrode slower than low-copper amalgams; it takes from 6 months to 2 years for high-copper alloys to self-seal their margins because they contain little or none of the most corrosion-prone phase, gamma 2. The most corrosion-prone phase in high-copper amalgams is the eta phase (Cu-Sn). [Anusavice 12th ed, p.379]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Best property of high copper amalgam as compared to low copper is
Explanation: The high-copper amalgams exhibit superior marginal integrity and reduced corrosion, primarily due to the elimination of the weak gamma-2 (Sn-Hg) phase seen in low-copper amalgams.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Rogue is used to
Option A: Prevent flow of solder to unwanted areas
Option B: Covers the metal surface and prevents access to oxygen so that no oxides can form.
Option C: Reduces any oxides present and exposes clean metal.
Option D: Dissolves any oxides present and carries them away.
Explanation: To prevent flow of molten solder onto adjacent areas, an antiflux such as rouge mixed with chloroform or graphite can be painted on these areas before heating substrate metals. There are three types of fluxes according to their primary purpose: Type I – Surface protection – covers the metal surface and prevents access to oxygen so that no oxides can form. Type II – Reducing agent – reduces any oxides present and exposes clean metal. Type III – Solvent – dissolves any oxides present and carries them away. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.389]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Greatest stress generated in a material till it follows a directly proportional relationship
Explanation: Elastic strain – Amount of deformation that is recovered instantaneously when an externally applied force or pressure is reduced or eliminated. Elastic modulus (also modulus of elasticity and Young's modulus) – Stiffness of a material that is calculated as the ratio of elastic stress to elastic strain. Proportional limit – Magnitude of elastic stress above which plastic deformation occurs. Toughness – Ability of a material to absorb elastic energy and to deform plastically before fracturing; measured as the total area under a plot of tensile stress versus strain. Yield strength – The stress at which a test specimen exhibits a specific amount of plastic strain. Ultimate tensile strength – Tensile stress at the instant of fracture. [Dental Materials Science by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.18]

Question: Calcination of CaSO4.2H2O at 130° leads to formation of
Explanation: Calcination between 110°C -130°C, gypsum partially dehydrates and converts to plaster or stone (Alpha/Beta Hemihydrate). Calcination between 130°C - 200°C, gypsum dehydrates and converts to hexagonal anhydrite. Calcination between 200°C - 1000°C, gypsum converts to orthorhombic anhydrite. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.183]

Explanation: Alternative Names for polysulfide impression material: Mercaptan impression material – by chemistry (presence of mercapton groups). Thiokol – first manufacturing company. Explanation: One of the chief disadvantages of the ZOE pastes is the possible stinging or burning sensation caused by the eugenol as it leaches out and contacts soft tissues. Zinc oxide can react with various carboxylic acids and form ZOE-like materials. Orthoethoxybenzoic acid (EBA) is a valuable substitute for eugenol in this regard. Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is added to denture base resins to prevent polymerization of polymer during storage
Explanation: Hydroquinone is added to denture base resins in small amounts by the manufacturer to prevent the accidental polymerization during transport and storage. [Dental Materials Science by Rama Krishna Alla 1st ed, p.53,252]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Acid base based polyacrylic cements have most important property of
Explanation: Acid base based polyacrylic cement means Zinc polycarboxylate cement. It is the first luting agent developed with the potential for adhesion to the natural tooth. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.318]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: In zinc polycarboxylate modified setting time and increased manipulative properties are due to
Explanation: The powder component of the cement contains mainly zinc oxide with some magnesia, tin oxide, bismuth oxide, and/or alumina. Stannous oxide is often added in small amounts to modify the setting time and improve handling characteristics of zinc polycarboxylate cement. These additions help in achieving more favorable working properties without compromising adhesion. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.318]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Radio-opacity in composite is due to presence of
Explanation: Ytterbium fluoride, Barium (Ba), Strontium (Sr), Zirconium (Zr), and Zinc glasses are added to composites to impart radiopacity. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.280]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Photo-initiator in dual cure composite is
Explanation: Composition of Dental Composites — Initiator and Activator systems: Initiator – Benzoyl peroxide (for Self-cure), Benzoin Methyl ether (for UV light cure), Camphoroquinone + tertiary Amine (for Visible light cure). Activator – N,N Dimethyl-Para-toluidine or tertiary Amine (for Self cure), UV light (365 nm) for UV light cure resins, Visible light (460–480 nm) for visible light cure resin. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.278]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Polycarboxylate cement adhesive failure is most commonly at
Explanation: Cohesion is an attraction process that occurs between similar molecules, primarily as the result of chemical bonds that have formed between the individual components of the adhesive or luting agent. Adhesion is the attraction process that occurs between dissimilar molecules, i.e., the bonding of one material to another, namely, an adhesive to a substrate, due to a number of different possible interactions at the adhesive-substrate surface interface. Polycarboxylate cement bonds chemically to enamel and dentin. The most likely failure occurs at the luting agent/prosthesis interface (adhesive). Remnants of the luting agent often remain on the opposing surface. Failure through the cement layer (cohesive) is unlikely because of the small thickness of the cement involved. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.333]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Titanium casting is done with
Option D: Arc Melting with an argon atmosphere
Explanation: Titanium has a high melting point (1668°C) and high rate of oxidation above 900°C. It requires a special casting machine with arc-melting capability and an argon atmosphere along with a casting investment consisting of oxides, such as MgO, ZrO2, or Y2O3, which are more stable than titanium oxide, to ensure acceptable castability. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.376]

Question: Most common problem faced with single etch adhesive system is
Explanation: Repeat from previous session — see explanation for Q10: phase separation due to hydrolytic instability of self-etch adhesive systems.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Thermal shrinkage in Phosphate bonded investment occurs due to release of
Explanation: The early thermal shrinkage of phosphate investments is associated with decomposition of the binder, magnesium ammonium phosphate, and is accompanied by evolution of ammonia, which is readily apparent by its odor. For gypsum investments, the shrinkage is caused by the transformation of calcium sulfate from the hexagonal to the rhombic form. However, some of the shrinkage is masked because of the expansion of the refractory filler, especially for cristobalite. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.208]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which is gypsum die hardener
Explanation: Increased hardness and abrasion resistance is especially important for die materials. Dies used to fabricate dental prostheses are often cast in Type IV or Type V gypsum material to produce a hard, accurate surface on which to make the wax pattern for the prosthesis. Coating the surface of the die with cyanoacrylates increases the abrasion resistance of gypsum die material.

Question: Silica whose inversion temperature is below fusion temperature
Explanation: Fused quartz is amorphous and glass like in character, and it exhibits no inversion at any temperature below its fusion point. It has an extremely low linear coefficient of thermal expansion and is of little use in dental investments. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.202]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Air abrasion uses
Explanation: Air abrasion for restoration preparation removes tooth structure using a stream of aluminium oxide particles generated from compressed air or bottled carbon dioxide or nitrogen gas. The abrasive particles strike the tooth with high velocity and remove small amounts of tooth structure. Efficiency of removal is relative to the hardness of the tissue or material being removed and the operating parameters of the air abrasion device. Parameters of air abrasion: air pressures generally range from 40 to 160 psi, with recommended levels of 100 psi for cutting and 80 psi for surface etching; the most common particle sizes are either 27 or 50 µm in diameter — larger particles allow faster work but result in comparatively larger-sized cavity preparations than 27 µm particles; higher particle flow rate allows more particles to abrade the working surface faster; the speed of the abrasive particles depends upon the gas pressure, nozzle diameter, particle size, and distance from the surface; typical operating distances range from 0.5 to 2 mm — further distances produce a more diffuse stream with diminished cutting ability; a number of variations in tip angulations and nozzle diameters are available for hard-to-access areas and operator comfort. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.244]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: What is percentage of gold in conventional type IV cast gold alloys?
Explanation: ADA specification no. 5 classified gold alloys as types 1 through 4, depending on the content of gold, palladium and platinum. The content of noble metals by weight ranges from 83% (type 1) to 75% (type 4). [Anusavice 12th ed, p.395]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Chromium is added to stainless steel as it provides
Explanation: Approximately 12% to 30% chromium by weight is added to carbon steel (commonly known as stainless steel). Chromium forms a very thin, transparent, adherent layer of Cr2O3 through a process called passivation, which provides a barrier to diffusion of oxygen and other corrosive species and it prevents further corrosion of the underlying alloy. [Anusavice 12th ed, p.408]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Best way to join cast titanium component
Explanation: Laser welding, plasma welding and infrared soldering methods are used for joining the cast titanium prosthetic points. Among these methods, laser welding gives better mechanical properties compared to others. Plasma welding and infrared soldering are used especially for the cases in which thicker parts need to be joined together as they increase the welded area thickness of up to 3 mm in the centre.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Highest slope in stress strain graph is seen in? (AIIMS NOV-17)
Explanation:
The slope of the stress strain graph is a measure of the relative rigidity or stiffness of a material. This is called elastic modulus or Youngs modulus or modulus of elasticity. Modulus of elasticity = stress/strain within proportional limit. Units = Giga Pascal or Giga Newton/m2. The highest slope means highest elastic modulus.

| Material | Elastic Modulus |
|---|---|
| Enamel | 84.1 |
| Dentin | 18.6 |
| Composite | 10.0 |
| Ceramic | 78.0 |

Enamel has higher elastic modulus (3-4 times) than dentin and is stiffer or more brittle, while dentin is more flexible and tougher; ceramics have higher modulus than polymers and composites. [Craig 13th ed, p.41]

Question: Galvanic current post placement of metal crown due to? (AIIMS NOV-17)

Option B: Dentinal fluid contains high concentration of H ions
Option C: Dentinal fluid contains high concentration of potassium than saliva

Explanation: Inability of a material to withstand plastic deformation before fracture is known as Brittleness. Ability of a material to absorb elastic energy and to deform plastically before fracturing is known as toughness. [Phillips' 12th ed, p.44]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: For cobalt-chromium hardness which test is used? (AIIMS MAY-18)
Explanation: The Brinell and Rockwell hardness tests have been used for determining the hardness of metals and metallic materials used in dentistry. Neither the Brinell test nor the Rockwell test is suitable for brittle materials. Vikat and Gillmore needle tests are for evaluating the setting time of gypsum products and cements. Cold bend test is one of the three methods used to determine ductility — the material is clamped in a vise and bent around a mandrel of a specified radius; the number of bends to fracture is counted, and the greater the number, the greater the ductility. The first bend is made at 90° from the vertical to the horizontal, but all subsequent bends are made through angles of 180°. Barcol test is used for measuring hardness of rubbers and plastics. [Phillips 12th ed, p.64]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Surface energy of which material is more than dentin? (AIIMS MAY-18)
Explanation:
Surface energy: The excess energy of molecules at the surfaces of materials above that of molecules found in the interior of a material.

| Material | Surface Energy (mJ/m2) |
|---|---|
| Enamel | 92 |
| Dentin | 87 |
| Teflon | 20 |
| Gold alloy | 51–54 |
| Ni-Cr | 48 |
| Commercial pure titanium | 50 |
| Acrylic denture resins | 46–54 |
| Water (liquid) | 72 @25°C |
| Mercury (liquid) | 486 @25°C |
| Saliva (liquid) | 53 @37°C |
| Dentin bonding agent (liquid) | 34–55 |

More is the surface energy, more is the wettability. Wettability can be enhanced by increasing the surface energy of the substrates (e.g., dentin, enamel, and synthetic materials). Since a clean, microroughened tooth surface has higher surface energy than unprepared tooth surfaces, organic adhesives are inherently able to wet and spread over such a surface. [Phillips' 12th ed, p.25]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Overheating of Co-Cr Solder alloy results in? (AIIMS MAY-18)
Option A: Yield strength increases & % age elongation reduces
Option B: Yield strength reduces & % age elongation increases
Explanation: Overheating during the soldering operation will cause (1) pits in the solder, (2) penetration or burning through thin sections, and (3) a loss of strength because of diffusion of the solder into the other metals or loss of fibrous microstructure. Underheating will cause pitting from the retention of unmelted flux and failure of the solder to flow and adhere to all surfaces; solder that is not well heated tends to "ball" and fails to spread properly. Both overheating and underheating will result in a weaker solder joint. For this reason, the proper and careful heating and fluxing of the solder are essential. [Craig 12th ed, p.544]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is not a method to speed up the rate of reaction of gypsum product? (AIIMS MAY-18)
Explanation: Control of the setting time of gypsum products: there are at least three mechanisms that can achieve such control. Solubility of the hemihydrate — if increased, supersaturation of the dihydrate is achieved faster, accelerating the rate of dihydrate crystal deposition. Number of nuclei of crystallization — the greater the number, the faster the dihydrate crystals will form and the sooner the mass will harden. Rate of crystal growth — increasing or decreasing this rate will accelerate or retard the setting time respectively. Note: Decreased rate of crystal growth (option D) retards the rate of reaction, so it is not a method to speed up the reaction. [Phillips' 12th ed, p.185]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is true about Dross? (PGI DEC.2017)
Option A: formed over ceramic teeth due to pressure
Option B: it is shiny surface over the alloy
Option C: formed by oxidizing portion of the flame
Option D: due to curing of denture at high temperature
Explanation: With a little practice, the clinician can readily detect whether the proper zone of the flame is in contact with the metal by observing the condition of the alloy surface. When the reducing zone is in contact, the surface of the gold alloy is bright and mirrorlike. When the oxidizing portion of the flame is in contact with the alloy, a dull film of "dross" develops over the surface — this cloudy surface indicates surface oxidation by improper positioning of the torch flame. [Phillip's 12th ed, p.222]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is true about phosphate bonded investment? (PGI DEC.2017)
Option A: The setting expansion is more as compared to gypsum bonded investment.
Option B: Type 2 is used for inlay only
Option D: phosphate is refractory component in phosphate bonded investment material
Explanation: Phosphate bonded investment: Theoretically, the reaction should entail a shrinkage, as in gypsum products, but in practice there is a slight expansion, and this can be increased considerably by using a colloidal silica solution instead of water. This solution allows phosphate investments to expand considerably rather than shrink according to predictions. Magnesium oxide and mono ammonium phosphate is the binder. Silica is the refractory. [Phillips 11th ed, p.309]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is incorrect: (PGI DEC.2017)
Option A: The stability of addition silicone remains same after 7 days as in 24 hours.
Option B: the residual segment of polysulphide can be detected with radiograph
Option C: tear strength values of hydrocolloids are about one-tenth of the values for the polysulfides
Option D: the set polyether impression exhibit least cell cytotoxicity score
Explanation: Option A — The stability of the addition silicone and polyether materials suggests that these impressions do not have to be poured with a gypsum product immediately. Research has shown that a cast produced from an addition silicone impression between 24 hours and 1 week was as accurate as a cast made in the first hour. Option B — acceptable degree of radiodensity would enable the detection of small fragments left inside gingival sulcus or root canals after impression procedures. The addition of chemical elements with high atomic numbers, such as lead, zinc, strontium, zirconium, barium and lanthanum, result in more radiopaque materials. Of all the classes of impression materials, polysulfides were the most radiopaque ones, apparently due to the presence of lead dioxide in the composition, which also acts as a catalyst of the setting reaction. Option C — Poly sulphides have highest tear strength followed by polyether, condensation silicone and addition silicone; hydrocolloids have less tear strength than elastomers. Option D — contact dermatitis and hypersensitivity potential exists with polyether impression material; cell cytotoxicity is lowest with polysulfide and highest with polyether impression material — making this statement incorrect. [Phillip's 1st SA, p.171,173]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: All are true regarding the eutectic composition of silver copper alloy except: (PGI DEC.2017)
Option B: The temperature at which the eutectic composition melts is lower than the fusion temperature of silver or copper.
Option C: The temperature at which the eutectic composition melts is higher than the fusion temperature of silver or copper.
Option D: Invariant transformation is seen in eutectic reaction.
Explanation: 72% Ag and 28% Cu by weight, which corresponds to point E, is known as the eutectic composition, sometimes called simply the eutectic. The temperature at which the eutectic composition melts (779°C) is lower than the fusion temperature of 100% silver or 100% copper (eutectic means "lowest melting") and is the lowest temperature at which any alloy of silver and copper is entirely liquid. [Phillips 12th ed, p.84]

Option C: Reduction in area in fractured region ends
Explanation: There are three common methods for measurement of ductility: the percent elongation after fracture; the reduction in area of tensile test specimens; and the maximum number of bends performed in a cold bend test. Barcol test is used for measuring hardness of rubbers and plastics, not ductility. [Phillips 12th ed, p.63]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Pseudoplastic materials are? (PGI JUNE-2017)
Option A: More rigid as the rate of deformation (shear strain rate) increases
Option B: Viscosity decreases with increasing strain rate until it reaches a nearly constant value
Option C: No change in viscosity with strain
Option D: Less viscous and more fluid under repeated applications of pressure
Explanation: Dilatant — Resistance to flow increases as the rate of deformation (shear strain rate) increases. The faster that fluids are stirred or forced through a syringe, the more viscous and more resistant to flow they become. Pseudoplastic — Viscous character that is opposite from dilatant behavior, in which the rate of flow decreases with increasing strain rate until it reaches a nearly constant value. Thus, the more rapidly that pseudoplastic fluids are stirred or forced through a syringe, the more easily they flow. [Phillips 12th ed, p.44]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following is true about Leucite based ceramic (AIIMS MAY-17)
Explanation: Alumina-reinforced ceramics: The alumina-reinforced feldspathic core was introduced by Hughes and McLean. The material consists of a feldspathic glass containing 40-50% alumina. The alumina particles are far stronger than the glass, are more effective in preventing crack propagation than quartz and act as crack stoppers. Whereas the flexural strength of feldspathic porcelain is at best some 60 MPa, this is raised to 120-150 MPa for the aluminous core porcelains. Alumina, 98% pure material, if used in high strength ceramics, will be having the strength in the range of 420-520 MPa. The main application of the alumina-reinforced porcelain jacket crown is for the restoration of anterior teeth. Although the improvement in strength is considerable, it is still insufficient to allow its use posteriorly and the construction of even a three-unit bridge is out of the question. Leucite-containing ceramics: Leucite-containing ceramics used in metal-ceramic restorations have a flexural strength of the order of 30-40 MPa (still etchable, unlike fully sintered/hot-pressed alumina-reinforced systems). [Richard Van Noort, Introduction to Dental Materials 2nd edition, p.240,244]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Brinell hardness number of a dental gold alloy is directly proportional to (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: Brinell hardness test: The Brinell hardness test has been used extensively for determining the hardness of metals and metallic materials used in dentistry. The Brinell hardness number is related to the proportional limit and the ultimate tensile strength of dental gold alloys. In this test, a hardened steel ball is pressed under a specified load into the polished surface of a material. The load is divided by the area of the projected surface of the indentation, and the quotient is referred to as the Brinell hardness number. Thus, for a given load, the smaller the indentation, the larger is the number and the harder the material. [Phillips 12th ed, p.64]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: What change occur in composite resin with change in size and number of filler particles (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: Functions of Fillers: Reinforcement — increases compressive strength, tensile strength, modulus of elasticity (i.e., stiffness or rigidity), and toughness; as the volume fraction of filler approaches approximately 70%, abrasion and fracture resistance are raised to levels approaching those of tooth tissue. Reduction of polymerization shrinkage/contraction — increased filler loading reduces curing shrinkage in proportion to filler volume fraction. Reduction in thermal expansion and contraction — increased filler loading decreases the overall coefficient of thermal expansion of the composite because glass and ceramic fillers thermally expand and contract less than do polymers. Control of workability/viscosity — the more filler, the thicker the paste; filler loading, filler size, and the range of particle sizes and shapes all markedly affect the consistency of a composite paste. Decreased water sorption. Imparting radiopacity — most often imparted by adding certain glass filler particles containing heavy metal atoms, such as Ba, Sr, or Zn, and other heavy-metal/heavy-atom compounds such as YbF3, which strongly absorb X-rays. [Phillips 12th ed, p.65]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Passivating layer on alloy is dissolved completely by (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: Aluminum, chromium, and titanium have high affinity for oxygen and they form protective oxide film, which prevents further oxidation and corrosion. This is called passivation. For soldering these alloys, the passivating film should be dissolved. Potassium fluoride used as a flux dissolves passivating film so that the solder can wet the parts. Flux is a compound applied to metal surfaces that dissolves or prevents the formation of oxides and other undesirable substances that may reduce the quality or strength of a soldered or brazed area. There are three types of fluxes according to their primary purpose: Type I: Surface protection — covers the metal surface and prevents access to oxygen so that no oxides can form. Type II: Reducing agent — reduces any oxides present and exposes clean metal. Type III: Solvent — dissolves any oxides present and carries them away. Fluxes for use with noble metal alloys are generally based on boric acid, boric anhydride, and borax. Chromium oxides that form on base metal alloys are more stable, and fluoride containing fluxes are used as solvents to dissolve chromium, nickel, and cobalt oxides. [Phillips 12th ed, p.389]

Zinc polycarboxylate bonds chemically with the tooth, and if failure occurs, it occurs at the cement prosthesis interface. [Phillips 12th ed, p.312]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: When stone cast is kept at temp >95°c (AIIMS MAY-18)
Option A: Dihydrate will change to monohydrate & cast will shrink
Option B: Monohydrate will change to dihydrate & expansion results
Explanation: Care of the Cast: In preparation, it is sometimes necessary to soak the gypsum cast in water for other procedures. When a dry cast is immersed in water, negligible expansion may occur if the water is saturated with calcium sulfate. If the water is not saturated, dissolution of gypsum will occur — for example, a stone cast immersed in a container under running water will lose approximately 0.1% of its linear dimension for every 20 min of immersion. The safest method for soaking the cast is to place it in a water bath with gypsum debris remaining on the bottom of the container to provide a saturated solution of calcium sulfate. If the storage temperature is raised to between 90°C and 110°C (194°F to 230°F), shrinkage occurs, along with loss of strength as the water of crystallization is removed and the dihydrate reverts to the hemihydrate form. As a rule of thumb, it is not safe to store or heat a stone cast in air at a temperature higher than 55°C (130°F). [Phillips 12th ed, p.278]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Transformation toughening in zirconia ceramic is because of transfer of (AIPG-2018)
Option C: Less stable to more stable tetragonal
Option D: Less stable monoclinic to more stable monoclinic
Explanation: Pure Zirconia has a monoclinic crystal structure at room temperature and transforms to tetragonal and cubic zirconia at elevated temperatures. The large volume expansion that occurs during the transformation of non-doped zirconia from cubic to tetragonal and tetragonal to monoclinic phases leads to structural expansion and high tensile stresses that cause zirconia to crack during cooling from the processing temperatures. To solve this problem, stabilizing oxides such as magnesium oxide (MgO), yttrium oxide (Y2O3), calcium oxide (CaO), and cerium oxide (CeO2) are added to zirconia. The most common stabilizer for dental applications is yttria (Y2O3). Transformation toughening: The structural stabilization of zirconia by yttria results in a significant proportion of metastable tetragonal phase. This metastable tetragonal phase strengthens and toughens the structure by a localized transformation to the monoclinic phase when tensile stresses develop at crack tips. The resulting volume expansion adjacent to the crack tips produces a high local compressive stress around the crack tips, which increases the localized fracture toughness and inhibits the potential for crack propagation. This phenomenon is called transformation toughening; it increases the flexural and tensile fracture resistance of stabilized zirconia prostheses and presumably the survival probabilities of zirconia-based restorations. [Phillips 12th ed, p.173]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: What happens if tap water having more of calcium and magnesium salts is used to mix Alginate (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: Tap water naturally contains certain levels of metallic ions, primarily calcium and magnesium. It has been shown that compared with distilled water for mixing of alginate impression material, the use of tap water with a high hardness may accelerate the setting of the alginate. If one observes that the setting time has decreased in a new office or clinic location, the effect of the hardness of the tap water on setting time should be considered as a possible cause. [Phillips 12th ed, p.210]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: A very high contraction occurs in the following investment by loss of alcohol & water (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: During the drying process of ethyl silicate investment material, the gel loses alcohol and water to form a concentrated, hard gel. As might be expected, a volumetric contraction accompanies the drying, which reduces the size of the mold. This contraction is known as 'green shrinkage', which is additive to the setting shrinkage. [Phillips 12th ed, p.226]

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Porosity due to gas inclusion during rapid solidification of molten alloy is (AIPG-2018)
Explanation: Porosities in noble metal alloy castings are classified as: (a) Solidification defects — localized shrinkage porosity, microporosity, suck-back porosity; (b) Trapped gases — pinhole porosity, gas inclusions, subsurface porosity, back pressure porosity. Both pinhole and gas inclusion porosities are related to the entrapment of gas during solidification; both are characterized by a spherical contour but differ in size — gas inclusion porosities are usually much larger than pinhole porosity. Many metals dissolve or occlude gases while they are molten; for example, both copper and silver dissolve oxygen in large amounts in the liquid state, and molten platinum and palladium have a strong affinity for hydrogen as well as oxygen. On solidification, the absorbed gases are expelled and pinhole porosity results. Larger voids may also result from the same cause, but it is more logical to assume that such voids are caused by gas that is mechanically trapped by the molten metal in the mold or by gas incorporated during the casting procedure.

Subject: Dental Materials
Question: Which of the following statement is correct based on the following image? [Proportional limit (PL), Ultimate tensile strength (UTS)] (AIIMS MAY-18)
Option A: A is more brittle than B and has more strength
Option B: A is more plastic than B and have more strength
Option C: B is more rigid than A
Option D: B less rigid than A and have more plastic deformation potential
Explanation: Shown in this figure are three stress-strain curves of materials with variable strength, elastic modulus or rigidity (slope), and percent elongation (ductility/plastic deformation). Material A is stronger, more rigid (highest slope), and more ductile than materials B and C. Material B has less ductility than material A and thus is more brittle. Material C has no ductility and is perfectly brittle; it is also the weakest of the three materials. [Phillips 12th ed, p.64]
